clinicalPearls: Classic triad of digital clubbing, periostitis of the long bones, and painful swelling of the joints and distal extremities
The secondary form is far more common and is usually a paraneoplastic marker of intrathoracic malignancy, especially non-small-cell lung cancer
Other secondary causes include chronic suppurative lung disease, cyanotic congenital heart disease, and cirrhosis, reflecting a cardiopulmonary or systemic drive
Periostitis produces a deep, burning bone pain, most marked in the tibiae, fibulae, radii and ulnae, with tenderness on palpation
Primary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy (pachydermoperiostosis) is a hereditary form with additional thickened, furrowed skin of the face and scalp (cutis verticis gyrata)
Radiographs and bone scintigraphy show symmetrical periosteal new bone formation along the diaphyses of tubular bones
Treatment of secondary disease centres on addressing the underlying cause, with NSAIDs and bisphosphonates used for symptomatic bone pain
reference.pathophysiology: Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy is characterised by proliferative periostitis and clubbing driven by dysregulated growth-factor signalling. In the common secondary form, platelet-derived and megakaryocyte-derived mediators, particularly platelet-derived growth factor and vascular endothelial growth factor, bypass the normal pulmonary filtration (through right-to-left shunting, lung disease or malignancy) and act on distal soft tissue and periosteum to stimulate vascular proliferation, oedema and new bone formation. The primary hereditary form (pachydermoperiostosis) arises from genetic defects impairing prostaglandin E2 degradation (mutations affecting the HPGD and SLCO2A1 genes), leading to sustained prostaglandin-mediated tissue and bone changes. The net result is periosteal new bone deposition, synovial effusions and the soft-tissue expansion of clubbing.
additionalDifferentials: Rheumatoid arthritis or other inflammatory arthritis
Venous stasis and chronic peripheral oedema
Bone metastases or primary bone tumour
additionalInvestigations: Chest radiograph and CT thorax to identify underlying lung malignancy or suppurative disease
Plain radiographs of long bones showing symmetrical periosteal new bone along the diaphyses
Bone scintigraphy demonstrating the 'tramline' or 'double stripe' cortical uptake
Echocardiography where cyanotic congenital heart disease or endocarditis is suspected
Liver function tests and imaging when hepatic causes are considered
redFlags: New clubbing and periostitis in a smoker, mandating urgent evaluation for lung cancer
Rapidly progressive symptoms with weight loss or haemoptysis
Signs of infective endocarditis or lung abscess as an underlying cause
Severe unremitting bone pain limiting mobility
reference.prognosis: The outlook in secondary disease is determined by the underlying cause, and symptoms often regress when a causative tumour or suppurative focus is treated or removed; the primary hereditary form is chronic but generally benign, causing cosmetic and musculoskeletal rather than life-limiting problems.
pitfalls: Treating the bone pain symptomatically without investigating for an underlying malignancy
Attributing clubbing to benign causes and missing early periostitis
Overlooking that resolution of secondary HOA can be a clue to effective treatment of the underlying disease
